## 1. GLOBAL MACRO OVERVIEW

The decisive new development since the June 1 report is the OECD's June Economic Outlook, published this morning, which for the first time formally quantifies the Iran war's economic damage in a dual-scenario framework. In the base (time-limited disruption) case, global growth slows from 3.4% in 2025 to 2.8% in 2026, recovering to 3.1% in 2027 — assuming the Hormuz disruptions resolve by mid-year. In the prolonged disruption scenario — no agreement until 2027 — global GDP slumps to 2.1% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027, rates "rarely seen outside major crises such as the 2008-2009 financial crash or the COVID pandemic." The OECD specifically warned that significant energy price shocks or shortages "would increase datacentre operating costs and constrain the supply of critical hardware used in AI systems" — a direct threat to the AI earnings supercycle that has underwritten equity markets [Source: https://www.cnbc.com/2026/06/03/oecd-warns-of-global-slowdown-as-iran-war-stymies-growth-prospects-.html]. US growth is now forecast to ease to 2.0% in 2026 and 1.8% in 2027; Japan is among the hardest hit, slowing to 0.6% in 2026 [Source: https://www.reuters.com/business/energy/oecd-says-protracted-war-could-drag-global-growth-push-up-inflation-2026-06-03/].

The Fed's hawkish pivot has moved from a minority view to near-consensus among vocal committee members. Cleveland Fed President Beth Hammack — a voting member who dissented at the April 28-29 FOMC meeting against language suggesting the next move would be a *cut* — stated Tuesday that rates may need to rise "soon" if inflation pressures continue. "Based on the data, I'm more concerned about the growing risks of persistently elevated inflation than the risks to full employment and also that monetary policy may not be sufficiently restrictive to bring inflation down to 2%," Hammack said, adding "if we wait for definitive evidence that high inflation has become embedded in the economy, it may require larger policy adjustments, at greater cost" [Source: https://www.reuters.com/business/feds-hammack-eyes-tighter-policy-if-inflation-doesnt-abate-2026-06-02/]. Interest rate futures markets are now explicitly pricing a rate *increase* at some point down the road, not just a hold [Source: https://www.kitco.com/news/off-the-wire/2026-06-02/feds-hammack-eyes-tighter-policy-if-inflation-doesnt-abate]. The 2-year Treasury yield sits at 4.05% as of June 1 [Source: https://fred.stlouisfed.org/series/DGS2], up 6 basis points from the prior report's 3.99%, consistent with this hawkish repricing.

Today's ADP report showed 122,000 private sector jobs created in May — slightly above some estimates — confirming labour market resilience that gives the Fed cover to prioritise inflation over employment. This directly pressures gold, which is "struggling below $4,500" as expectations that the Fed will raise interest rates by year-end continue to mount [Source: https://www.kitco.com/news/article/2026-06-03/gold-price-struggling-adp-says-122k-jobs-created-may]. Friday's official Non-Farm Payrolls report is now the next key binary for the Fed path.

The ECB is moving toward its own rate hike next week. The WSJ reported this morning that the ECB "looks set to raise its key interest rate next week, dusting off a tactic it last employed in 2011 as it seeks to send a strong message on inflation at a time when the eurozone economy is at risk of a slide into recession" — explicitly comparing the current situation to the ECB's 2011 mistake of hiking into a recession [Source: https://www.wsj.com/pro/central-banking/ecb-rate-hike-risks-repeat-of-earlier-misstep-0a36da7c]. Simultaneously, Indian and Indonesian central banks are facing similar dilemmas, with markets debating whether the RBI will follow Indonesia's shock 50bp hike to defend the rupee [Source: https://www.cnbc.com/amp/2026/06/03/-like-indonesia-indias-central-bank-may-hike-rates-to-defend-its-currency.html].

Equity markets are pulling back as the OECD warning lands. The S&P 500 is down 0.39% to 7,580.24, the Dow -0.58% to 51,009.76, and the Nasdaq 100 -0.23% to 30,591.19 [Source: Yahoo Finance (^GSPC), (^DJI), (^NDX)]. Notably, Nasdaq is outperforming on the day — as of the prior session's MarketWatch reporting, the S&P 500 and Dow were set to extend their longest win streaks of the year, but today's OECD shock and Hammack hawkishness have reversed that [Source: https://www.marketwatch.com/livecoverage/stock-market-today-dow-jones-s-p-500-nasdaq-ai-optimism-nvidia-new-pc-superchip]. The VIX has risen 3.99% to 16.40 [Source: Yahoo Finance (^VIX)], a modest escalation but below the acute stress levels that would signal a regime change. The Nikkei, however, surged 2.5% to 68,402.13 — its strongest print in this data series — likely driven by continued JPY weakness and delayed reaction to AI semiconductor momentum [Source: Yahoo Finance (^N225)].

### Disputed

- **"The 2-year Treasury yield sits at 4.05%, up 6 basis points from the prior report's 3.99%"**: The bundle confirms 4.05% as of June 1, but the prior report's 3.99% value is from a previous session not in the bundle. The directional claim (up 6bp) cannot be verified against bundle data alone. Not disputed on today's 4.05% reading, only the delta claim.

- **Strategy sold "$2.5 million worth of bitcoin"**: The CoinDesk article in the bundle states Strategy "sold $2.5 million worth of the token." However, the CNBC article in the bundle describes it only as "a small amount of bitcoin" without specifying a dollar figure. The $2.5 million figure appears in CoinDesk and is accepted, but the report should note this is an unusually small amount for a company of Strategy's size — the wording "$2.5 million" could be confused with $2.5 billion by readers. The data bundle does not contradict the figure, so this is a flag rather than a hard dispute.

- **"The S&P 500 is down 0.39% to 7,580.24… essentially flat versus the June 1 close of 7,581.04"**: The report claims the June 1 S&P 500 close was 7,581.04. The Barron's article in the bundle shows an S&P 500 level of 7,575.06–7,575.35 during Monday June 1 trading. The report's June 1 close figure of 7,581.04 is not verifiable from the bundle and may be slightly off, though the "essentially flat" characterisation is broadly consistent with the Barron's intraday data.

- **"NZD/USD dropped sharply… the largest single-session NZD/USD move in recent weeks"**: The bundle confirms -0.99% today, but there is no historical NZD/USD move data in the bundle to verify the "largest in recent weeks" claim.
